title: Master Class | Danish Declined! | Chess Speedrun | Grandmaster Naroditsky

moves.spoken: We're White against a lower-rated opponent, so let's play very aggressively — we still haven't had the chance to unveil a legitimate Danish Gambit. e4, e5.
d4 — the Danish, offering the center to blow the position open.
Instead of grabbing, he plays the knight to c6. So what do we do here?

My favorite move: d takes e5. The short reason is that it clarifies the center — the knight to f3 would just transpose into a Scotch, but I think capturing is best, both to open things up and because the knight that recaptures on e5 will be awkwardly placed.
The knight recaptures on e5, and this knight is really not well placed — it's exposed to a whole series of tempo-gaining attacks.
We develop naturally with the knight to c3, getting a piece out and keeping options open.
Black offers a trade with the knight to f6 — a non-committal move; we don't have to decide about trading yet.
f4 — you give an exoskeleton to your position. When you only develop pieces without supporting pawns, those pieces float; the pawn advance both kicks the e5-knight and gives the center a spine.
The knight retreats to c6, and now the advance is associated with a very strong follow-up: e5, chasing the f6-knight back.
He has to go all the way back to g8, losing a ton of tempo, and his position already looks grim.
We bring the other knight out, the knight to f3, developing with gain of time.
His best try is d6, striking at our advanced e5-pawn.

Here's a tip: once your pieces are out and the opponent's king is stuck, a queen trade doesn't kill your attack — a lot of your attackers aren't the queen. The bishop to b5 pressures the pinned defender and steers toward exactly that.
A queen trade would have cost him his castling rights and left his king a sitting duck, so instead he plays the bishop to d7, breaking the pin.
We castle — the king still has a nice pawn shell, and the fact that we advanced the f-pawn doesn't spoil it. He replies d takes e5.
We recapture, f takes e5, and he's done us a big favor by opening the f-file straight at his king.
Now his king is going to be in real trouble. He gives a check with the bishop to c5.
We tuck the king to h1, out of the checks and ready to attack.
It looks like Black will finish developing before we do — the knight to e7 — but that doesn't matter, because we're about to whip up a very quick attack on that king.
What active moves can we play? The first thing my mind's eye sees is that loose bishop on c5 — so the knight to e4 jumps in, hitting it.
Black slides the bishop to f5, and we take the bishop — the knight captures on c5, winning the bishop pair and staying on top.
Black plays a6, poking at our bishop.
The bishop simply drops back to c4, and we're basically winning.
He offers the queen trade, queen takes on d1, and we recapture with the rook. This raises a very contentious question — is it good to trade when you're up material?
Black finally castles into safety.
My take: don't feel you HAVE to simplify just because you're ahead. A lot of blunders come from ignoring the other features of the position. We calmly play c3.
Black brings a rook to d8, contesting the file.
Don't go blind to attacking chances just because you're trying to simplify — the bishop to g5 eyes the dark squares.
Black slips the bishop to c2.
I do have a clean chance to trade rooks, so why not — the rook takes on d8 with check. We give up the d-file, no big deal.
Black recaptures on d8.
It's an endgame and we can snap off another pawn — the knight takes on b7, a free pawn.
Black tries the rook to d1 with check; we trade it off. A word of caution I've shared: don't chase too many extra pawns when you're already up a stack of pieces.
But if there are free pawns with no consequences, absolutely take them: the bishop comes to d3, bishops are traded, Black plays h6, and the bishop scoops up on a6 — more material for nothing.
Now we simplify: Black shuffles the knight to c8, our bishop comes to f6, the knight reroutes to e7, and the bishop takes on e7, peeling off another defender.
Black recaptures with the knight on e7.
The knight comes to c5, centralizing and supporting the passed e-pawn.
Black jumps the knight to f5, trying to blockade.
We push the passed pawn to e6 — it's about to become a monster.
Black lunges with the knight to e3. We'll just retreat our bishop and then win this pawn — the game is over, we're up a piece.
e7 is correct — the pawn is one step from queening.
Black tries the knight to g4, but there's nothing left; he resigns.
In the meantime let's analyze — even grandmasters get tunnel vision, and it's a big problem worth talking about.
Back to the start: d4, and the knight-c6, d-takes-e5 structure again.
Let me respond to the idea that the knight is 'in the center' after it recaptures on e5 — is a central piece automatically good?
The knight to c3 — and here's the general point: why is it even good for a piece to be central? What is it about the center?
The catch is that the weaknesses of the position haven't been defined yet, so sitting on a central square means a bit less here — there's nothing concrete for the knight to grip.
In this analysis line the knight jumps to d5, showing how a 'central' piece can be poked.
Because your opponent has plenty of resources to kick pieces away — c6 shoves the knight — you learn that centralizing too early backfires.
So it's more important to develop quickly than to plant your pieces in the center prematurely.
And there's another reason to prefer flexible development here.
I can play a move like the knight to f3 and essentially offer a trade — and if you trade knights, you've moved that same knight several times, handing me a big development lead.
